title: A transformation is judged by what it keeps: orientation, composition and linking
summary: The first three course animations ask what a map does to space. A map can fold a grid (the Jacobian determinant changes sign), a flow of an ODE composes like a clock (the semigroup law), and some quantities, such as a linking number, survive any smooth deformation without tearing. Companion static figures show the determinant of a squaring map, a two-to-one fold, trajectories that cannot cross, and linked rings under a flow.

media.alt: Three stills from course animations. A rectangular grid squeezed toward its left edge with some cells shaded as folded; two panels of trajectories that settle onto y equal plus one and minus one, with a start and now column of points; and a 3D view of a blue ring linked with a deformed orange loop beside a flat line of the linking number near minus one.

read_the_figure.question: Which property of a map survives the deformation, and where does it fail?
read_the_figure.axes: S001: x and y in plain dimensionless coordinates; the grid is the image of a regular square grid. S002: left panel time against y, right panel the starting column of points and the same points after time t. S003: left a 3D scene of two closed curves, right the computed linking number against isotopy time t from 0 to 1.
look_at: S001: the title reports the share of cells with negative determinant (33 percent at t = 0.50). Shaded cells have been turned inside out; a smooth, invertible map would show none.

S002: blue filled dots (apply phi_s, then phi_t) and the gold rings (apply phi_(t+s) once) should lie on top of each other. The title gives the mismatch, 4.7e-15 at t = 1.02: round-off, not a real difference.
S003: the black line is the linking number computed numerically while one ring is deformed. A flat line means an invariant; its value stays within about 0.001 of -1.
In all three, the title or axis is a numerical check printed by the script, not decoration.

Companion figures. Jacobian parallelogram: a deformed grid and small parallelograms at three points; the right panel colours det D Phi = 4 (x^2 + y^2), zero only at the origin (marked with a star). The map behaves like squaring a complex number.
Fold, two to one: upper half-disc (blue) and lower half-disc (orange) have images that overlap exactly, f(x, y) = f(-x, -y): a half disc already covers the whole image, so the map cannot be inverted.

Flows cannot cross: thirteen trajectories of a one-dimensional ODE never meet (minimum gap 0.0091); the second panel shows the target map g(x) = -x, which would require every path from -1 to 1 to cross every path from 1 to -1, impossible for an ODE flow. The figure attributes this obstruction to a published result (Dupont, Doucet and Teh 2019).
Linked rings under a flow: three snapshots of two rings deformed by a nonlinear flow; the linking number stays at about -1 (the wiggle in the right panel is of order 1e-4).
read_the_figure.proves: Each still shows one numerical certificate: a determinant sign count (S001), a semigroup mismatch at round-off level (S002) and a nearly constant linking integral (S003). Together they say which words in 'smooth, continuous, invertible' actually matter.
if_wrong: Cells with negative determinant: the map is not locally invertible there; an inverse or a normalizing-flow change of variables would fail.
A semigroup mismatch far above round-off: the integrator, not the maths, is composing differently (step sizes or a non-autonomous field).
A drifting linking number: the deformation tore a curve through the other, or the quadrature is too coarse.
must_check: That the title or readout is stated (percent folded, mismatch, value of the invariant).
That the same grid or the same initial points are used before and after.
That the map family parameter t is labelled and runs over the whole range.
For S003, that the invariant is computed rather than assumed.

terms.meaning: A rule F that sends each point of the plane or space to another point.
A family of maps F_t that changes continuously from one map (t = 0) to another (t = 1).
The local area (volume) scale factor of a map. Its sign says whether orientation is kept or flipped.
A place where det J changes sign: the map is not invertible there.
The map phi_t that sends an initial state to its state a time t later along an ODE.
Flowing for s and then for t is the same as flowing for t + s.
A deformation through maps that are each one-to-one, so a curve never crosses itself or another curve.
An integer that counts how often one closed curve winds around another. It cannot change under an isotopy.

remember: det J > 0 keeps orientation, det J < 0 flips it, det J = 0 collapses an area to zero.
A map is locally invertible exactly where det J is not zero (inverse function theorem).
The flow of an autonomous ODE satisfies the semigroup law and is invertible: run time backward.
A numerical check at round-off size (1e-14 to 1e-16 in double precision) means 'equal'.
Invariants are what a deformation keeps; they tell you what a learned transformation may not change.

steps.title: Area scale factor of a grid map
steps.note: Each small grid cell is mapped to a parallelogram whose area is |det J| times the original. Cells that shrink drift together in the picture; cells whose determinant is negative are drawn turned inside out.

steps.title: An illustrative homotopy that folds
steps.note: This is an example family, not necessarily the exact map in the animation. At t = 0 it is the identity (det = 1). For t > 0 the determinant becomes negative for x below -(1-t)/(2t): a fold line appears and the left part of the grid is flipped.

steps.title: Why the semigroup law holds
steps.note: Uniqueness of the solution through the point y(s) means continuing for a time t is the same curve as starting at x and running for s + t. The figure checks this on a column of starting points.

steps.title: The semigroup law in a case you can write down
steps.note: Exponentials add in the exponent, so composition of flows is addition of times. Any ODE solver that fails this by more than round-off is composing different step sizes.

steps.title: Linking number as a double integral
steps.tex: \mathrm{Lk}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\oint\!\oint\frac{(\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)\cdot(\mathrm d\mathbf r_1\times\mathrm d\mathbf r_2)}{\lVert\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2\rVert^{3}}
steps.note: The Gauss integral is integer-valued for two disjoint closed curves. Evaluated numerically along an isotopy it stays near the same integer; the small wobble in the figure is quadrature error, not real change.

steps.title: What a flow of a field cannot do
steps.note: The Jacobian determinant of an ODE flow is an exponential and so never negative. A flow can squeeze a grid but it cannot fold it. That is why a fold, as in the first still, is not the time-t map of any ODE.

steps.title: Why a flow cannot swap two points on a line
steps.note: In one dimension, paths from -1 to 1 and from 1 to -1 must cross by the intermediate value theorem; uniqueness of solutions forbids two trajectories from meeting. So the map x to -x is not the time-t map of any ODE on a line.

worked.title: Where does the illustrative family fold at t = 0.5?
worked.problem: For F_t(x,y) = ((1-t)x + t x^2, y) at t = 0.5, find the x at which det J = 0 and say which side is flipped.

solution.text: The determinant is the x-derivative of the first component, since the second component is y.
For x below -0.5 the determinant is negative.

worked.answer: The fold line is x = -0.5; every cell to its left is orientation-reversed.

analyze.q: S001 shows 33 percent of cells with negative determinant at t = 0.50. Does that percentage have to rise steadily with t? Argue from the sign of det J along a homotopy.
analyze.hint: A determinant changes sign only by passing through zero.

analyze.q: S002 lists a mismatch of 4.7e-15. State two reasons it is not exactly zero, and what size would make you suspect a bug.
analyze.hint: Double-precision round-off is near 1e-16 per operation.

analyze.q: In S003 the linking number is about -1.0004 and not exactly -1. What does that say about the numerical method, and what about the mathematics?
analyze.hint: Separate an invariant from its estimate.

evaluate.q: A normalizing flow needs det J at every point. Which of the three figures warns most directly against a learned map that is not built as an ODE flow?
Is a sign-count of folded cells a sufficient test of invertibility?
evaluate.hint: A map can be locally invertible and still send two far-apart points to the same place.

create: Write the homotopy of a map that rotates the grid by an angle growing with t. Predict the folded fraction for all t and check it against the Jacobian.
Design an experiment with two linked rings in which the numerical linking integral does change, and say what you would do to the curves to make it happen.

checks.q: What does the sign of det J tell you?
checks.answer: Positive: orientation preserved. Negative: flipped (a fold has been crossed). Zero: area collapsed and the map is not locally invertible.

checks.q: For y' = -y compute phi_0.5(phi_0.3(2)) and phi_0.8(2).
checks.answer: Both equal 2 exp(-0.8), about 0.899. They agree because the exponents add.

checks.q: The title says 33 percent of cells have det < 0 at t = 0.50. Where in the picture do you look for the fold line?
checks.hint: The cells are drawn orange or shaded.
checks.answer: At the boundary between the shaded (negative) and unshaded cells: the determinant passes through zero there, and the grid lines pile up against the fold.

checks.q: Can a flow of an ODE produce the map in S001?
checks.hint: What is the sign of det of a flow map?
checks.answer: Not at a time when det is negative. The flow's Jacobian determinant is an exponential of an integral and is always positive, so a fold cannot be the time-t map of an ODE. It would have to be a different kind of map.

checks.q: Name one quantity you would add to a learned-coordinate pipeline as a certificate, in the style of these titles.
checks.answer: For example the minimum of |det J| over a sample grid, or the semigroup mismatch of the learned flow, printed in the figure title.
